title: Baby Lawrence's funeral at the Church of the Holy Communion
summary: Tap dancers including Peg Leg Bates, Harold Kromer and Bunny Briggs gathered at Baby Lawrence's funeral, where each tapped joyful noises and said Amen.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Didn't he preside over the Baby Lawrence funeral?
Can you tell me about the Baby Lawrence funeral?

Yes. Well, as I say, he held that at the -- the Baby Lawrence funeral idea at the Church of Emmanuel up there on 88th and -- I'm glad that you asked that -- and Lexington, you know. And one of the tap dancers ranks came out, you know, a line of them, you know, the ones that was in retirement. They came, you know. And they were in the parish, you know.

So, and their way of -- what you say -- giving the dead to the rest, you see -- this they rank got up, you see. See, and in the rank was one of the Four Badmen which was known as Peg-Leg Bates, see. And he got up and there was someone in -- yeah, Harold Kromer, the jazz monitor. He was there. I know he got up. And Lon Chaney.

Well, it was like some kind of squad, do you understand? A rank I'd say. I like to say a rank because that's what the guard officiates in the world, you see. And there was some speakers, you see. See, that's to just name a few of them. There was this -- one of Baby Lawrence's proteges -- I'm quite sure, but he didn't get enough of the tap dancer's dream, you know. He was very touched by it. He's still with us, you see. That's Bunny Briggs. And another great friend, you see, but we lost him, you see. See, they all didn't last

too long after him -- this one. He got -- he was already suffering, you see. I mean the businessman of rhythm, you see. His name was Lawrence also, you know, and he did his, you know, askance for the tap dancer's dream.

What I'd like to know as bravery, (unintelligible) because he gave us some -- he left something for us to be, to become, you see, in the future. I mean art itself, it must retain these specimens (unintelligible). That he wanted to be -- remain remedial, see. And I think that we can continue to have it lasting, and to set records, to make books.
What happened at the funeral, Chuck?

Well, each one of us, we spoke to God footagely (unintelligible) you see by tap -- in tap dancing. Joyful noises, you see. Then we all said Amen, you see. It was like a prayer for his receivership, you see, when he get back to the Maker, you know. So -- and the Reverend Ginzo, you see, he really was the whole antidote of it all, you see, because he allows us to make these joyful noises, you know. And degree of our faiths more better, you know, because that's it, you see. They don't want us to become molested in any kind of a passion, you know. They don't want us -- our -- they don't want our compassions to be fradulent in any kind of way.
-- his story. So, the Jazz Vespers --
Reverend Ginzo asked us to come up there, and he introduced.

He mentioned -- he said who we were, each one. It was about -- approximately about 30 or 20 guys, you know. Different ages. And we'd come up and revie, you know. And Like an (unintelligible) or so, you know, and stay at attention, you see, because eventually we were going to go, you understand, after the passions, emotions like they say. But we said -- we said happy reawakening, see. Tap dancer's dream.
